passage:
“Mama! Mama! Manoj took a biscuit before lunch!” Arohi ran into the kitchen, eyes shining.

“Did he?” Mama said, stirring the dal. “How do you know?”

“I saw! Dadi saw too. He hid it under the pillow.”

Manoj appeared at the door, red-faced. “It was only one.”

Mama looked at Arohi. “Thank you for telling me. Did you want a biscuit too?”

Arohi looked at the floor, then up. “I wanted you to say I'm good.”

“You're good either way,” said Mama. “Come and help me with the rotis.”

qa.q: What did Arohi say Manoj took before lunch?
qa.a: Arohi said Manoj took a biscuit before lunch.

qa.q: Why did Arohi run to tell Mama about the biscuit?
qa.a: Arohi was eager for Mama's praise and wanted to hear Arohi is good, so telling was a way of getting approval; the shining eyes show Arohi's excitement.

qa.q: What choice did Mama make that changed the mood in the kitchen?
qa.a: Mama thanked Arohi for telling, asked about Arohi's own wish for a biscuit and said Arohi is good either way.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel standing at the door red-faced?
qa.a: Manoj probably felt embarrassed and caught out, and perhaps annoyed that Arohi told.

grounding: A young child announces who did what to win adult approval and test rules, closer to reporting than malice.

passage:
Teacher's note, Nursery B, Wednesday. During free play Wasim came to me four times in ten minutes. “Jasleen threw a block.” “Ayaan took the red one.” “Jasleen said a bad word.” Each time he studied my face. He wasn't upset. He seemed pleased to have something to tell.

I thanked Wasim for telling me and said I would look when someone was hurt. I asked Jasleen quietly what had happened: a tower had fallen. Then I gave Wasim a job, tidying the red blocks. I'll keep watching whether reporting is how he asks for attention.

qa.q: How many times did Wasim come to the teacher in ten minutes?
qa.a: Wasim came to the teacher four times in ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Wasim studying the teacher's face after each report suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Wasim wants to see whether the news earns approval, and is pleased to have something to tell.

qa.q: What did the teacher do after thanking Wasim?
qa.a: The teacher asked Jasleen quietly what had happened and gave Wasim a job tidying the red blocks.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel hearing the reports from the block corner?
qa.a: Jasleen might feel embarrassed or worried about getting into trouble, even though a tower had simply fallen.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young child repeatedly reporting what others did, seeking adult approval, and how the teacher responded.

passage:
“Mummy! Mummy! Vinita didi ate the chocolate from the fridge!” Jatin ran into the kitchen, eyes shining.
Mummy turned from the stove. “Did she?”
“Yes! I saw! And she said don't tell!” He stood very straight, waiting.
Vinita appeared at the door, face red. “He's a tattle-tale!”
“I'm not! I'm telling the truth!” Jatin looked at Mummy. “Am I good?”
Mummy knelt. “Thank you for telling me, Jatin. Didi and I will talk. And next time, you can ask didi to share.”
Jatin nodded, a bit disappointed there was no prize.

qa.q: What did Vinita didi eat?
qa.a: She ate the chocolate from the fridge.

qa.q: What did Jatin want when he asked "Am I good?"
qa.a: He was eager and hopeful for Mummy's approval, even a prize, for reporting.

qa.q: How did Mummy handle Jatin's tale well?
qa.a: She thanked him calmly, said she would talk with didi herself, and gave him a kinder idea for next time, without praising telling tales.

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt when Jatin told?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and cross, her face red, calling him a tattle-tale.

grounding: Shows a young child telling tales about his sister mostly to win his mother's approval, sensing that news is social currency.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Class KG-2, Wednesday.
Ojas has started reporting every small rule-break. Today alone: “Shalini took two biscuits.” “Pinku touched the fish tank.” “Rohan didn't wash his hands.” Each time, he looks at my face to see what I will do.
It doesn't seem mean. He looks proud when I say “thank you”. Shalini told him, “You're always telling!” and moved away from him at snack time.
I now ask, “Is anyone hurt? If not, tell your friend directly.” I will also make Ojas water-bottle helper, so he has another way to feel useful.

qa.q: What did Ojas say Shalini took?
qa.a: He said, "Shalini took two biscuits."

qa.q: What does Ojas looking at the teacher's face suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he is eager and hopeful for approval, checking whether telling earns praise.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's new question a good idea?
qa.a: It separates real danger from small tales and helps Ojas speak to friends directly, while the helper job gives him another way to feel proud.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt about being reported?
qa.a: Shalini was annoyed and a bit hurt, telling Ojas he's always telling and moving away.

grounding: A teacher notes a young child who reports every small rule-break mainly for adult approval, not malice.

passage:
In Dadi's courtyard in the village, Alka came running. “Dadi! Bhavna is on the guava tree! You said no climbing!”
Dadi looked up from the grain she was cleaning. Bhavna's legs were dangling from a branch.
Alka stood very straight. “I told you first. I'm good, na?”
“Bhavna, come down slowly,” Dadi called. Bhavna climbed down, glaring at Alka. “Tattle-tale!”
Alka's smile wobbled. She looked at Dadi, then at Bhavna.
Dadi pulled Alka into her lap. “Thank you for telling me about the tree. It's high. Next time, you can also tell Bhavna first. She's your friend.”

qa.q: Where was Bhavna?
qa.a: Bhavna was on the guava tree.

qa.q: How did Alka feel when Bhavna called her a tattle-tale?
qa.a: She felt unsure and a little hurt; her proud smile wobbled.

qa.q: What did Dadi say that could help Alka next time?
qa.a: She thanked Alka for the tree, since it was high, and suggested Alka also speak to Bhavna first as a friend.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Alka's telling?
qa.a: Bhavna felt annoyed and betrayed, glaring at Alka for reporting her.

grounding: Shows a young child telling on her cousin to win approval and test the rule, closer to reporting than malice.

passage:
In the kindergarten in Osaka, Dalia marched up to Ms Tanaka before snack time. "Yuki took two crackers. And Ren splashed at the sink. And Hana didn't wash her hands." She stood very straight, waiting.
Ms Tanaka knelt. "Thank you, Dalia. Is anyone hurt or in danger?"
Dalia thought. "No."
"Then let's see if Yuki wants to share the extra cracker."
Dalia looked back at Yuki, who was holding both crackers and frowning at her. Dalia's smile wobbled.

qa.q: How many crackers did Yuki take?
qa.a: Yuki took two crackers.

qa.q: Why did Dalia stand very straight after telling?
qa.a: Dalia felt proud and was hoping for praise, waiting for Ms Tanaka to approve of her reporting.

qa.q: How did Ms Tanaka's question help Dalia?
qa.a: Asking "Is anyone hurt or in danger?" teaches Dalia the difference between telling to keep people safe and telling to get someone in trouble.

qa.q: How did Yuki seem to feel about Dalia's report?
qa.a: Yuki seemed annoyed, frowning at Dalia while holding the crackers.

grounding: Shows a young child announcing who broke small rules, mostly for adult approval, already sensing that news about others has social value.
